data.title: Barack Obama, Kamala Harris call for government action on AI development
data.description:
Barack Obama, Kamala Harris call for government action on AI development

Arlette Saenz, CNN
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 12:40 am UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris on Monday were among the latest high-profile Democrats to call for greater government action to address artificial intelligence as some industry leaders call for a slowdown in the technology's development amid growing public concern.

"We need government – and specifically our leaders in Washington – to get proactive in coming up with concrete proposals, laws and regulations that deal with serious safety concerns, anticipate AI's impact on jobs and our kids, and make sure that AI's benefits are widely spread," Obama said in a statement Monday night. "Given what we know about technology, we can't stuff AI back in a box. But we can collectively determine how it's developed and how it's used, rather than sitting back and letting AI and its fallout happen to us."

The debate around artificial intelligence has ramped up in recent days, with some politicians and tech executives calling for greater government regulation of the industry while President Donald Trump has deemed the concerns about AI a "HOAX" and part of a "SICK conspiracy."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In a sign of the issue's political potency, Obama, speaking at a private fundraiser alongside House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, last week urged Democrats, including those considering running for president in 2028, to put AI at the center of their agendas.

Harris, who is seen as a possible 2028 contender after falling short of winning the presidency in 2024, chimed in on Monday with support for a slowdown to allow regulation to catch up with the technology.

"The frontier of artificial intelligence is advancing at an alarming speed. Over the weekend, industry leaders voiced support for an idea that the American people and many AI researchers in their own labs have been calling for: We must responsibly slow the pace of frontier AI development," she said on X. "A slowdown is critical in order to ensure AI serves the public interest."

Harris called for Congress to establish a federal oversight agency and urged Trump, her former rival, to work towards an international treaty to address AI.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The United States must continue to lead the world in developing AI technology even as we seek to impose common-sense safety standards," she said. "This means that the president must do his job to protect America's interests by pursuing a treaty with countries like China to stop dangerous uses of AI, limit the speed of its development, and adopt global standards for testing."

Trump, however, has fiercely rejected calls for a slowdown or increased regulation in a series of social media posts in recent days downplaying safety concerns and hyping up the need to stay competitive with China.

"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" Trump said on Monday. "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies! There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China."

Trump's stance appears to be at odds with the growing public concerns about AI's development. Over the weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei penned a lengthy essay calling for a slowdown in the development of artificial intelligence. In an exclusive interview with CNN's Anderson Cooper on Saturday, Amodei called on industry leaders to work together to avoid "the wrong paths" and the possibility of AI harming humanity.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Both Obama and Harris acknowledged the immense potential of the technology on Monday but underscored the need to pace development.

"I'm not an AI accelerationist who believes it will lead to some techno-utopia, and I'm not a doomer who thinks it will inevitably lead to humanity's destruction," the former president said. "But whether this technology results in amazing breakthroughs in medicine, energy and education or unleashes huge economic disruptions, greater inequality, and potential catastrophe will depend on the choices that we make right now – choices that should be made not just by the companies involved, but by all of us."

Pete Buttigieg, a former Transportation secretary whose name is also in the mix for 2028, has also emphasized the stakes of the technology and over the weekend argued that the government need to address AI "head on."

"AI is moving quickly. And for Congress to just sit on its hands, for the White House to do nothing real is something that is deeply dangerous to the American people and the world," Buttigieg said on NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday. "There need to be safeguards. There need to be rules. There need to be limits. There needs to be a kill switch on rogue AI. You can set up frameworks that can be adjusted and changed every 30 days."

This headline and story have been updated with additional remarks from Obama.

data.title: New Zealand agencies missed red flags in child kidnapping case: inquiry
data.description:
New Zealand agencies missed red flags in child kidnapping case: inquiry

AFP News
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 1:21 am UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

New Zealand authorities failed to act on prior warnings that a man who went on the run with his kids for four years had a stash of guns and fears he would kidnap his children, an inquiry into a case that drew global headlines found Tuesday.

Tom Phillips was shot dead by police in September 2025 after nearly four years hiding with his three children in the rolling hill country of the North Island's Waikato region.

He had eluded capture by setting up several camps in dense bush and despite several sightings by the public and on CCTV.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

A report on Tuesday into the handling of the case by authorities found a number of red flags were raised about Phillips prior to the kidnapping -- the second time he had disappeared with his children.

"The harm caused by Tom Phillips isolating the children from family, friends and society was underplayed, minimised or overlooked by agencies for significant periods," the report found.

"Our agencies did not take all practical steps to protect you," government minister Louise Upston said to his children.

"For that we are deeply sorry."

The 211-page report looked at the time before the children were taken in December 2021, through to the moment they were recovered after the deadly shootout in September last year.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Phillips first disappeared with his three children in September 2021 for 18 days.

He abandoned his vehicle on a beach, below the high tide mark, and the report said police believed "Tom Phillips had staged his and his children's death".

When he emerged from the bush 18 days later, he was charged with wasting police resources.

Police at the time were "seriously concerned that he might take the children away again", the report said -- fears that were not passed on to the Ministry for Children.

They also failed to identify and seize his firearms after he lost his licence around the same time, the report said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Those additional steps could have contributed to recovering the children sooner," it found.

In the two months before Phillips took the children again, social workers also ignored concerns raised by their older step-siblings.

One specifically asked if the agency "would be held responsible if the children went missing again".

The other provided an affidavit to the agency which was never read.

A supervisor for the ministry admitted that had they read the statement they "would have challenged Tom", and that it "read terribly", the report found.

Ministry of Children chief executive Amanda Malu admitted the report was "difficult and at times harrowing reading".

"We did not listen in the way we should have, and this family deserved better from us."

data.title: Trump dismisses AI safety alarm, says US already has tools to police industry
data.description:
Trump dismisses AI safety alarm, says US already has tools to police industry

By Courtney Rozen and Katharine Jackson
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 12:59 am UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Courtney Rozen and Katharine Jackson

WASHINGTON, Sept 14 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Monday that the U.S. already has guardrails in place to regulate and prosecute AI companies, appearing to play down concerns expressed by industry leaders about the misuse of artificial intelligence harming people.

Public alarm about the potential danger posed by ‌AI is growing, after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said last week he had resigned, in part because the "people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all ‌by the end of the decade." AI-related stocks fell worldwide on Monday after leaders of some of the industry's largest companies called for slowing the pace of the technology's development.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) ​PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that China would benefit from the doubt being cast on AI development. Trump is scheduled to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping next week in Washington.

Reuters previously reported that the two countries were planning a separate meeting in mid-September to discuss the risks of AI, led by lower-level government officials.

U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters on Monday that he expects Trump to meet with AI executives this week or "early next week." The meeting would focus on "the responsibilities of the companies to maintain safety and what role, if ‌any, the government has to play in that."

Vice President JD Vance ⁠separately told reporters on Monday he is skeptical of the AI executives calling on the U.S. government to regulate the sector.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I feel a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate ⁠them," Vance said.

Trump on social media said the AI industry's call for regulation is a "hoax."

AMODEI'S ESSAY

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in an essay published on Saturday that the U.S. government should write regulations requiring independent audits of the most advanced AI tools, known as "frontier" models.

Reuters reported on Monday that three U.S. senators are working on a bill that would require AI companies to demonstrate they are taking reasonable precautions to keep ​their ​tools from causing harm, with the specifics still being debated.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In his essay, Amodei outlined a three-step framework he ​said was intended to slow the pace of AI development and create more ‌time to manage its risks. The proposal was immediately endorsed by several other executives at major AI companies, including Elon Musk, who runs xAI, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

U.S. Senator Mark Warner, a Virginia Democrat and a leader on technology legislation, spoke with Amodei and Altman about AI safety concerns over the weekend, his spokesperson said.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang addressed the AI safety concerns during the All-In Summit in Los Angeles on Monday.

"There's just a whole bunch of stuff: pausing, pacing. Those are all voluntary things that they could do if they feel that their company is out of control," Huang said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Huang took a phone call from Trump during the event and put him on speaker for the audience. During the roughly five-minute call, Trump said data centers make people and ‌states wealthy, calling them the "oil of the next 20, 25 years".

Trump also said critics of AI development were "playing ​right into the hands of a lot of people that don't want to see it happen, and that could ​be political people, that could also be China".

"We're not going to let that happen," ​Trump said, drawing agreement from Huang.

Trump has so far resisted concerns about AI and has largely embraced tech companies in his second term. The tools intended ‌to keep AI safe had already been used on Amodei's Anthropic, he ​added without elaborating.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The Trump Administration has stopped AI 'people' ​from doing bad, or potentially bad, 'things,' like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a 'perfect little angel' — and we will continue to do so," Trump wrote on social media.

Anthropic's media team did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters about Trump's statement.

The Trump administration is in a dispute with Anthropic over AI safety and the battlefield. ​U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth blocked the company from certain military ‌contracts because the company refused to allow the U.S. to use its Claude AI models for domestic surveillance or autonomous weapons.

Anthropic sued in a California court, and ​a U.S. judge sided with Anthropic in one lawsuit on August 27.

(Reporting by Courtney Rozen and Katharine Jackson in Washington, Bhargav Acharya in Toronto; Assistance by David ​Morgan in Washington; Editing by Doina Chiacu, Bill Berkrot, Nia Williams, Aurora Ellis and Michael Perry)

data.title: Accenture to pay $25 million to settle US government allegations over DEI
data.description:
By Kanishka Singh

WASHINGTON, Sept 14 (Reuters) - IT consulting firm Accenture will pay $25 million to settle U.S. government allegations over diversity practices, ‌which President Donald Trump's administration has targeted in his second term ‌in office.

"Accenture shall pay to the United States $25,000,000, inclusive of civil penalties and interest on ​the Settlement Amount at a rate of 4% per annum from September 9, 2026," the settlement agreement made public on Monday said. It was signed by the U.S. Department of Justice and Accenture.

The Trump administration has penalized public ‌and private organizations, from ⁠government agencies to universities, over DEI practices that civil rights advocates say help address historic inequities for marginalized groups ⁠such as women, the LGBT community and ethnic minorities.

The White House casts DEI as anti-merit and discriminatory against white people and men. Trump has signed executive ​orders asking ​federal contractors and subcontractors to eliminate ​DEI. Civil rights groups say ‌such steps roll back social progress.

Many U.S. companies scaled back or modified diversity policies after Trump's orders.

Deloitte agreed to pay $21.5 million to settle a DOJ probe over diversity practices, according to an agreement made public in August. IBM agreed to pay $17 million to settle a similar U.S. government probe, ‌an agreement revealed in April.

The Justice Department ​had alleged Accenture took race and sex into ​consideration when it made hiring ​and promotion decisions to achieve demographic goals.

Accenture said it ‌complied with applicable laws and that ​the resolution agreement ​did not constitute an admission of liability.

"We have cooperated with the government's review, and we are pleased to put this matter behind us ​to avoid the costs ‌and resource demands of prolonged litigation," an Accenture spokesperson said.

The ​settlement agreement said Accenture denied engaging in discrimination.

(Reporting by Kanishka Singh ​in Washington; Editing by Muralikumar Anantharaman)

data.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump’s plan to limit mail-in voting in midterms
data.description:
Supreme Court rejects Trump’s plan to limit mail-in voting in midterms

John Fritze, CNN
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 12:10 am UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

The Supreme Court on Monday rejected President Donald Trump's controversial plan to change how mail ballots are sent to voters across the country, rebuffing a proposal that election officials warned would have had catastrophic consequences if allowed to take effect for this year's midterms.

In one of the most significant cases to appear on the court's quick-turn docket in years, a majority of the justices blocked the procedure that would have given the US Postal Service the unprecedented power to withhold potentially millions of mail ballots. Even some GOP election officials cautioned that the proposal could lead to chaos and mass disenfranchisement.

The court said that the administration "is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge" but offered little explanation in its three-sentence, unsigned order. Conservative Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The decision is a significant loss for the president, who for years has railed against mail voting with false allegations of extensive fraud, while continuing to vote by mail himself.

The administration had framed its proposal as a "modest" change to postal regulations intended to protect against that alleged fraud. Trump's critics, however, described the maneuver as an unconstitutional power grab that the US Postal Service wasn't even fully prepared to carry out.

CNN has reached out to the White House for comment.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a member of the court's conservative wing, wrote a concurrence explaining that he thought the proposal may be within the authority of the USPS, but that "state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

That appeared to be a recognition of a flood of briefs from state and local election officials who argued there simply was not time this late in the election process to implement the president's order. But it also suggested that Kavanaugh could be gettable for the president, along with Alito and Thomas, to try the changes for a future election.

In his dissent, Alito said he didn't believe the practical concerns of implementing the rule raised by many election officials was enough for the states and voting rights groups that challenged the rule to win.

"The government has a strong interest in enforcing the rule, and implementing it will also 'en­hance the visibility of Federal Ballot Mail' in order to better detect election fraud," Alito wrote. "On the other side of the balance, the plaintiff States invoke the practical ef­fects of implementing the rule close to the midterm elec­tions. I take that problem very seriously, but it is not enough to convince me to deny the application."

"That Hail Mary pass is unlikely to be successfully completed here," Alito wrote. "The Postal Service has broad authority to regulate the mail."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In addition to the Democratic-led states and voting rights groups that challenged the proposal, a bipartisan coalition of election administrators, former governors and others warned the justices about last-minute changes to mail ballot procedures. The Postal Service rule required states to upload mass amounts of data on voters to an online portal that wasn't yet online. And it required changes to ballot envelopes that had already been purchased, and that an increasing number of states had already begun to drop in the mail.

USPS rule now a dead letter

The Democratic states and voting rights groups that sued over the order praised the court's decision late Monday.

"Trump's attempt to sabotage the 2026 elections has failed," said Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold, a Democrat.

The administration argued that the changes were needed to secure the ballots and ensure that only eligible voters receive them. But a coalition of two dozen Democratic-led states and voting groups have described the effort as a power grab by a president who has long falsely alleged widespread voter fraud in mail ballot systems.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Filed last week, the high-profile emergency appeal was the third time the Trump administration raced up to the Supreme Court on the policy. In late August, the court allowed the president to proceed, though it did so for technical reasons that had to do with the timing of the lawsuit challenging the policy. A lower federal court blocked the changes from going into effect days later.

Under the Constitution, it is states and Congress that determine voting procedures, not the White House nor the post office.

The president's order required states to submit lists of eligible voters to the US Postal Service. The agency would be barred from delivering ballots mailed by states to people not on those lists. It also required states to use tracking barcodes on ballot envelopes. And it "prioritized" federal prosecution of state election officials who send or receive ballots to non-citizens or others ineligible to vote.

While the Supreme Court was weighing the legal issues, a Postal Service whistleblower came forward with a stark series of warnings. The whistleblower's report made clear that not only would one ballot be withheld if there was a problem with the barcode on its envelope, but rather officials would decline to deliver the entire batch of mailings that envelope was a part of. The whistleblower also described a rushed process to stand up an online data sharing system that the person said could make the complicated plan even more vulnerable to potential mass disenfranchisement.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump has for years touted conspiracy theories about mail voting as a way to discredit the 2020 presidential election that he lost. But improper voting remains exceedingly rare, and the administration has never provided evidence of widespread fraud on a scale that could influence the outcome of the 2020 election, or any other contest.

Multiple federal courts rejected the proposal. Over the weekend, a US District Judge Carl Nichols, a Trump nominee in Washington, DC, became the latest to put the USPS rule on hold for the midterms.

This story has been updated with additional details.

data.title: EU extends Russia sanction deadline
data.description:
EU extends Russia sanction deadline

AFP News
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 12:29 am UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

EU countries on Monday delayed a deadline for prolonging sanctions on Russia over the Ukraine war after France pushed for billionaire Alisher Usmanov to be removed from a blacklist.

The European Union blacklist of almost 3,000 individuals and entities -- which needs to be extended every six months -- was set to expire by Wednesday.

But ambassadors from the 27 EU member states pushed back the deadline one week after the late efforts from Paris to remove 73-year-old Uzbek-Russian metals tycoon Usmanov drew opposition.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Usmanov, a former major shareholder in Arsenal football club, was placed on the EU sanctions list in 2022 over what Brussels said were his close ties to the Kremlin.

"Consultations will continue, and further discussions are expected to be held," a spokesman for Ireland, which holds the EU's rotating presidency, said.

"Renewal of the listings is essential to continue undermining Russia's war machine, and keeping the pressure on those individuals and entities supporting, enabling and benefitting from it," the spokesman said.

EU diplomats said France took its counterparts by surprise by supporting a Slovakian request to take Usmanov off the list.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Diplomats said France did not give a clear reason beyond saying it was for "national security".

French officials confirmed they were seeking to remove Usmanov but did not detail their motives.

The Financial Times reported that Paris was making the push as part of a prisoner release deal involving several French citizens held in Azerbaijan, citing people familiar with the issue.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told AFP Monday only that "discussions are currently underway at the technical level in Brussels" and he expected them to conclude soon.

Diplomats from multiple EU countries said there was widespread reluctance for the bloc to be seen to be weakening its sanctions on Moscow.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

EU countries had been instead been looking to extend the length of the sanctions from six months to a year as they seek to keep pressure on Moscow.

The EU's sanctions include key figures including Russian President Vladimir Putin and Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, in his daily address, said: "It is definitely not the time to lift sanctions."

He added: "It is definitely not the time to rescue Russian oligarchs from sanctions. And it is definitely not the time for Europe to be giving gifts to Russia."

data.title: Trump dismisses AI alarms as a ‘HOAX’ — worrying White House officials
data.description:
Trump dismisses AI alarms as a ‘HOAX’ — worrying White House officials

Kevin Liptak, CNN
Mon, 14 September 2026 at 11:55 pm UTC
7 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

President Donald Trump spent Monday angrily rejecting calls from AI industry leaders for more government regulation on their cutting-edge models, making clear in a daylong string of social media posts he considers outpacing China and preserving AI-driven economic gains a higher priority than addressing growing public concerns.

Trump asserted a "SICK conspiracy" was afoot to undermine AI and claimed his oversight alone was enough to prevent models from going rogue. He called concerns a "HOAX," comparing the technology to the "Global Warming Scam" and the investigation of possible ties between his campaign and the Russian government. He also renewed his support for the data centers that power AI, despite their political unpopularity.

"The people that say AI is going to destroy the World, and that Data Centers are bad for your neighborhood, are the same people that said, just a short time ago, that the World would be extinguished by 'Climate Change,'" Trump wrote. "That HOAX never worked out for them, and now they're on to the next one."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump had posted six times on the matter by Monday evening, reflecting an issue that has quickly come to dominate political debate in the United States. He also placed a telephone call to Jensen Huang, the CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, to declare "the robots will not be taking over." Huang, a fellow opponent of industry regulation who was appearing onstage at a conference, put the call on speakerphone to amplify Trump's rebuttals.

The president's fierce pushback after a weekend spent at his golf resort in Ireland reflected a series of conversations he held with advisers and industry leaders who rejected the new calls by AI leaders for a global slowdown in development, according to people familiar with the matter. Trump told reporters over the weekend he used AI personally, but advisers say that extends mostly to generating images for posting on his social media pages.

Others inside the administration, including Vice President JD Vance, also cast doubt on the motivations that led executives, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, to call for more government oversight.

The stance has placed the White House at odds with growing public skepticism of AI and wedged vulnerable Republicans in a tough spot as they work to show voters they take the concerns seriously. Even some White House officials privately say they are worried about Trump's apparent lack of concern about AI's dangers — a position he's held for months and has been seemingly unmoved by industry warnings.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Over four consecutive days, the president has continued to downplay the need for new safety checks. He said Monday the US already has "tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!"

"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" Trump wrote on Truth Social, where he frequently posts AI-generated images and videos of himself.

He said the administration had already prevented AI companies from doing "bad, or potentially bad, 'things,'" and singled out Amodei for "now pretending to be a 'perfect little angel.'"

Later Monday, Trump called Huang, who has been publicly skeptical about AI doomsday predictions, while the tech leader was speaking a summit in Los Angeles. After Huang put him on speakerphone for the crowd, Trump said he was genetically predisposed to understand the issue because his uncle taught at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I also have common sense about AI," Trump added. "The robots will not be taking over. The AI will not be taking over the rest of the world. The whole thing is a hoax."

Trump has long espoused the benefits of AI, and many industry leaders have contributed financially to some of his priority projects, including his inaugural fund and the ballroom he is building at the White House.

AI's meteoric growth has also led to major stock market gains and buoyed the manufacturing sector through data center construction, both of which Trump points to as evidence of a strong economy under his watch. He called AI "the golden goose" in another social media post Monday.

Yet fears about the technology's potential to eliminate jobs and AI data centers' impact on communities have led to a souring in public sentiment. Recent warnings about security concerns have amplified calls for new guardrails.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Vance cast doubt on calls from industry executives for more AI regulation, warning it could amount to a "Trojan horse" by companies that could benefit from new restrictions.

"There are obvious risks to AI, there are some benefits to AI," Vance told reporters at Joint Base Andrews. "I have to say, personally, I feel a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them."

Still, Vance acknowledged the new technology comes with risks and said he hopes the White House and Congress would work together to develop guardrails.

"I don't think Americans should be scared of anything. I think we have to be mindful that there are risks, there are downsides to anything, and that's certainly true of AI," Vance said before boarding a plane for a campaign swing.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

White House officials said there would likely be meetings set up this week with administration experts on AI and cybersecurity to discuss potential new regulations on the technology. House Speaker Mike Johnson, speaking Sunday, said he hoped to convene talks with Trump, lawmakers and AI executives to plot a path forward. He said Monday that meeting would probably occur in a week or two, though he cautioned against a rush for congressional action.

"There'll be a deliberate discussion about the responsibility of the companies to maintain safety and what role, if any, the government has to play in that. But again, we do not want to jump in," the Louisiana Republican said. "The reflex of legislative bodies is to cover things up with red tape and hyper-regulation. If you do that, then you lose your edge, and that is a national security concern for the American people."

Senate Majority Leader John Thune similarly said he believes there should be "guardrails" for AI to ensure safety but prefers a "light touch" from Washington so the US stays competitive with China.

While there is broad agreement from many lawmakers that AI could use basic regulation, they recognize that they face an uphill battle to get something done soon. Sen. Bernie Sanders said Monday that Congress is "at best, a slow-moving institution. But I would hope that we rise to the occasion."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Republican Sen. John Kennedy said that "nothing is going to happen, in my opinion, until after the midterms." However, he noted he still intends to introduce legislation this week aimed at requiring companies to have an AI "kill switch."

"It just says all of you have to have a kill switch so you can shut this thing down if your model becomes the Terminator," the Louisiana lawmaker told reporters.

A new effort was also underway among US officials to beef up planned discussions about AI with Chinese leader Xi Jinping when he travels to Washington for a state visit next week. Trump has been eagerly preparing for the occasion, including by finishing up renovation work on the North Portico and a new helipad on the South Lawn.

In one of his Monday social media posts, Trump claimed that Xi "announced that China will be doing absolutely nothing to stand in the way of AI, or its future."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

When the two men last met in Beijing in May, they discussed AI guardrails but produced limited results. Last week the Chinese Ministry of Commerce said the two leaders had agreed to set up an intergovernmental dialogue on AI.

This story and headline have been updated with additional developments.

CNN's Ellis Kim, Manu Raju, Alison Main, Morgan Rimmer and Ted Barrett contributed to this report.

data.title: Houthis strike Saudi targets anew as talks over Strait of Hormuz stall
data.description:
Houthis strike Saudi targets anew as talks over Strait of Hormuz stall

By Timour Azhari
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 12:07 am UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

FILE PHOTO: Vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam

1 of 3
FILE PHOTO: Vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, September 2, 2026. REUTERS/Stringer/File Photo

By Timour Azhari

RIYADH, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis launched a new wave of attacks on Saudi Arabia and were digging into positions on the western coast of Yemen along the Red Sea, Yemeni officials said, as urgent deliberations took place in Riyadh over how to respond to their lightning advance.

Meanwhile, Gulf Arab states postponed ‌planned talks with Iran, raising concerns the Middle East conflict could spread further and threaten global oil supplies.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Houthis on Monday said they fired dozens of missiles and drones ‌at a military airbase in Khamis Mushait in southern Saudi Arabia, targeting aircraft hangars, radar systems, runways and ammunition depots in retaliation for Saudi airstrikes in Yemen.

Saudi authorities issued emergency alerts there and in three other southern cities. Thirteen civilians ​were wounded in the Houthi attacks, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said.

The Houthi advances in recent days, including the taking of Perim Island at the mouth of the Red Sea, have put further pressure on Saudi oil exports after an aerial attack on Thursday knocked Saudi Arabia's east-west pipeline offline. Riyadh blamed the pipeline attack on Iranian-backed militias in Iraq.

Saudi Arabia built the 1,200-kilometer (745-mile) pipeline across its territory from the Gulf to the Red Sea in the 1980s to bypass the Strait of Hormuz when it came under threat from the Iran-Iraq war at that time.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Traders said a prolonged shutdown of the Saudi pipeline could cut off ‌as much as 4% of global oil supply while the strait ⁠is largely blockaded. Riyadh has not said when operations might resume.

Responding to the Houthi offensive, the Saudi and Yemeni air forces have stepped up aerial bombardment of Houthi targets, including around the historic Red Sea port of Mocha, but the Houthis have maintained effective control over almost the entire western coast of the country ⁠along the Red Sea, the officials with Yemen's internationally recognised government said.

"The Houthis are being put under heavy pressure. They in turn are putting more and more pressure on the Saudis, increasing their campaign of missile and drone attacks," one of the Yemeni officials said.

Crude oil prices rose more than 4% on Monday before settling about 1% higher.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

AMERICANS HESITANT TO STEP IN

The renewed Yemen conflict poses another challenge for U.S. President Donald Trump.

Three sources have ​told ​Reuters that Washington has so far resisted Saudi requests for direct military intervention beyond intelligence support. Trump said ​over the weekend he had spoken with the Saudi crown prince and that ‌the Houthis had also contacted Washington urging it to stay out of the conflict.

Saudi state media reported that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met U.S. regional commander Admiral Brad Cooper in Jeddah on Monday.

Saudi Arabia has led a coalition battling the Houthis since 2015, but the conflict had largely quietened under a ceasefire in recent years. Fighting reignited this month, with the Houthis pushing back forces aligned with the internationally recognised government.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

HOPES FOR DIPLOMACY FADE

Oman had been due to host a meeting on Monday with Iran and Gulf states to discuss negotiations aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war carried 20% of the world's oil exports. But Oman announced that the meeting had been postponed. Iran said the postponement was at the request of Saudi Arabia.

Trump on Monday repeated his frequent claim ‌that Iran was eager to make a deal quickly, but Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security ​Council, called the president's message a distraction, saying on X, "No talks until Iran's conditions are met."

Underscoring the volatility of shipping through ​the region, conflicting reports circulated about how and when an oil tanker was damaged.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Without giving ​a date, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said the Panamanian-flagged oil tanker El Gaia was hit by sea mines as it passed through a prohibited zone south ‌of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Fars news agency reported on Monday.

But the ​U.S. military's Central Command immediately said the report was ​false and the tanker was "struck by an Iranian missile last month and rendered inoperable."

The United Nations' International Maritime Organization reported El Gaia was damaged on Saturday, but did not say how, and that two seafarers were missing.

Reuters could not immediately contact the ship's owners in Dubai to verify any of the accounts.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The world's most important oil shipping lane has been mostly ​shut down since the war began on February 28 as Iran has ‌threatened vessels that transit the waterway without its authority.

"The IRGC Navy firmly declares that the Strait of Hormuz is closed and still under our smart control," the Revolutionary Guards ​said in the statement.

(Reporting by Timour Azhari in Riyadh, Jana Choukeir, Eman Abouhassira, Elwelly Elwely, Nayera Abdallah in Dubai, Yasmine Ghania and Yomna Ehab in Cairo, Daphne ​Psaledakis in Washington, and Lisa Baertlein in Los Angeles; Writing by Daniel Trotta; Editing by Cynthia Osterman)

data.title: Supreme Court Blocks Trump’s Attack On Mail Voting — For Now
data.description:
Supreme Court Blocks Trump’s Attack On Mail Voting — For Now

Paul Blumenthal
Mon, 14 September 2026 at 11:57 pm UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

The Supreme Court on Mondaydeclined to lift a preliminary injunction blocking the implementation of President Donald Trump's effort to undermine mail voting weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

"The Government is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge to the District Court's preliminary injunction. And the equitable factors applicable for obtaining emergency relief from this Court do not favor a stay," the ruling read. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote a brief concurrence, while Justice Samuel Alito wrote a more lengthy dissent, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas.

Politics: Supreme Court Slaps Down Republicans' Attempt At Dismissing Late Mail-In Ballots

The case came to the Supreme Court after the administration appealed a Sept. 4 decision by District Court Judge Indira Talwani blocking the Postal Service from implementing a rule that would change state mail voting rules. The Trump administration filed appeals seeking to stay Talwani's decision in the First Circuit Court of Appeals on Sept. 5 and the Supreme Court on Sept. 6. The appeals court rejected the administration's stay request on Sept. 9.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The Supreme Court read the Constitution," Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes, a Democrat, told HuffPost ahead of the ruling. "It's none of his business how elections are run."

The rule would have required states to completely overhaul their mail voting systems in the middle of an ongoing election. It required states to use USPS barcodes on all mail ballots and submit lists of mail voters to the federal government ahead of time. If states failed to comply, the Postal Service would refuse to deliver those ballots.

Experts have warned that the rule would have blocked eligible American citizens from legitimately voting.

In briefs to the court, election officials from both parties argued that implementing the rule now would be "impossible." Ballots had already gone out to voters in North Carolina on Sept. 4. Any attempt to do so "will almost certainly lead to mistakes, delays, and confusion for both voters and election officials," a group of current and former Republican election officials wrote in one brief.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

"No election office, at any level of government, has budgeted for the work the Rule requires," the brief from GOP election officials stated. "And none have the time or the means to fully train or test on this Rule. That simply cannot be done midstream of this election."

Potential problems with the administration's plan had already emerged before it even launched a portal meant to handle the Postal Service's matching of names to submitted lists of mail voters.

Politics: Trump Visits Ireland, Putin Warns Europe Against Sending Troops To Ukraine: Live Updates

A whistleblower told Congress that a "secretive" and rushed process for USPS to implement the rule could lead to mass disenfranchisement. The whistleblower's report stated that the rule would lead the Postal Service to refuse to deliver all mail ballots in a single batch if one ballot's barcode presented an issue. That meant that one error could lead to 10,000 ballots being rejected for delivery.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Postal Service even rejected the envelope design for 32,000 mail ballots in Leon County, Florida, on the technicality that the return address was 0.014 inches too close to a label stating "return service requested." The Leon County clerk said he would send them out anyway, assuming the court would strike down the rule.

With the Supreme Court's decision to keep the district court order in place, the administration's effort to undermine mail voting in this election is likely dead.

"This was an attempt by this administration to decide who gets to vote that was illegitimate," Fontes said. "That's not the way America works."

Politics: Trump Ally Can Challenge Rules For Mail-In Ballots, Supreme Court Rules

But Trump has attempted to make it work that way. He has claimed that every election Republicans lost over the past two decades were tainted by imaginary fraud. And, when he lost one of those elections in 2020, he attempted to overturn the results, first in the courts and then through a coup attempt on Jan. 6, 2021.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

This is not the only voting-access case before the Supreme Court. On Sept. 8, the administration appealed to the court for permission to use a Department of Homeland Security database to verify voters' citizenship. A federal judge had blocked use of the database, which the administration argued it needs to combat voter fraud, on the grounds that it violated federal laws on privacy, governance of administrative agencies, and the Social Security Act.

The Postal Service rule was just one of many efforts by Trump in his second term to undermine elections — all of which have been blocked by the courts. He may yet try another attempt in the final weeks before Nov. 3.

Related...

  • Trump Administration Makes Another Appeal To The Supreme Court To Allow Mail Ballot Restrictions

  • Trump's Scheme Could Wreck A Cherished American Institution

  • New Mail Voting Rules Moved Forward Despite USPS Officials' Concerns About Mass Disenfranchisement

data.title: Iran reports commercial vessel struck in Strait of Hormuz
data.description:
Iran reports commercial vessel struck in Strait of Hormuz

Laura Sharman, Ibrahim Dahman, Rupert Neate, Jennifer Hansler, CNN
Mon, 14 September 2026 at 11:12 pm UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Iranian state media has claimed an Iranian commercial vessel was struck in the Strait of Hormuz late Saturday, killing one person, amid an ongoing battle between the US and Iran for control over the crucial energy chokepoint.

It comes at the same time as Iran-backed rebels in Yemen step up attacks and advance in their efforts to control a second vital waterway in the region, which could put further pressure on global oil prices.

The Hormuz attack, which the state-run Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB) said injured four, took place near Qeshm Island in the strait.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Iran's official Islamic Republic News Agency (IRNA) quoted the Qeshm governor as blaming a "terrorist enemy" for the attack.

The US has not commented on the reported attack. CNN has reached out to US Central Command for comment.

The US military has previously struck Iranian-flagged vessels as it maintains a blockade of Iranian ports and faces the renewed threat of Iranian ballistic missiles launched at its warships.

Qeshm Island, which is about 14 miles from the Iranian port city of Bandar Abbas, is key to Iran asserting control over traffic through the vital Strait of Hormuz, through which about 20 million barrels of oil passed every day before the war. Traffic remains about 90% below pre-conflict levels.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

On Sunday, India's Ministry of External Affairs said that the MT El Gaia, a Panamanian-flagged vessel with 14 Indians among its crew, was attacked off the Omani coast.

"Of the 14 Indian crew onboard, 13 Indians have been rescued so far," ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on X. "Search and Rescue operations for the missing Indian national are continuing."

Iran's military said the El Gaia hit a sea mine while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian state media on Monday. US Central Command quickly branded the claim as "false," asserting that the ship was struck by an Iranian drone over the weekend. CNN has reached out to the Indian Ministry of External Affairs for comment.

Separately, another vessel was hit by an unknown projectile in the strait late Saturday, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) center.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

UKMTO said a fire broke out and that local authorities were helping evacuate crew members. It did not provide details of which state has registered the vessel.

Talks on the Strait of Hormuz

Tehran on Monday criticized the postponement, at Saudi Arabia's behest, of planned talks on the Strait of Hormuz between Iran and Arab states of the Persian Gulf. Iran said it would now decide how to announce a new arrangement reached with Oman governing the waterway.

The meeting, planned for Monday, would have offered participating countries an "opportunity" to free the region from foreign interference, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said, according to IRNA.

Top diplomats from Gulf Arab states were expected to meet with Iran's foreign minister in Oman on Monday to discuss the management of maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, Baghaei said Saturday.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

However, Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi said Sunday that the talks were postponed "in the interests of consensus." Bahrain had said it would not attend, and it was not clear which other nations would be there had the talks proceeded.

Asked about the postponement, a Gulf official said Saudi Arabia submitted amendments because it had concerns that the proposed language could effectively establish a new status quo that would not be acceptable to it or the other Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states.

Baghaei said Monday the meeting was "suddenly" postponed at Saudi Arabia's request due to "developments in Yemen," which he characterized as "a diversion from the root causes of this crisis."

Iranian state media reported that officials are working closely with Oman to find a new date for the meeting, according to a translation from Reuters. Iran has been negotiating for months with Oman, which controls the opposite bank of the strait, over a deal that could govern shipping through it.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Oman's energy minister, Salim Al Aufi, said Monday that disruption to the strait is probably a short-term situation and should stabilize in the medium term, according to Reuters.

Iran had played down the prospects of a breakthrough. President Masoud Pezeshkian told broadcaster India Today TV on Saturday: "The waterway would be opened up on the condition that the US will terminate its blockade."

Ebrahim Azizi, head of the Iranian parliament's national security committee, said on X: "As long as ⁠the American side does not accept all of Iran's conditions, dialogue and negotiation are of no use."

A senior Iranian official told CNN on Sunday that the talks aimed to lay the groundwork for improved regional security and work on "safe maritime routes."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"However, this agreement does not imply an automatic reopening of the Strait of Hormuz," the source said. "The strait will not become secure until the US fulfills its obligations and halts its naval blockade and economic warfare."

Iran-backed Houthis attack Saudi base

Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthis attacked the Saudi Arabian cities of Khamis Mushait, Abha and Taif on Monday with missiles and drones, injuring 13 civilians and damaging seven homes and two vehicles, according to Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a Saudi military spokesperson, who vowed a response.

On Sunday, the Houthis claimed responsibility for an attack on a Saudi military base in the Sharurah region bordering Yemen.

The Houthis have recently stepped up their fighting against Yemen's Saudi-backed government and have expanded their area of control to the vicinity of a vital Red Sea waterway that links Asia to Europe.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Houthis' spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said a "barrage of ballistic missiles and drones" was used to target "weapons depots and command and control rooms," but he did not specify when the attack took place.

On Saturday, the Houthis claimed that Saudi forces launched 129 airstrikes across Houthi-held areas of Yemen.

Last week, the Houthis captured Perim Island, at the mouth of the Red Sea. The island splits the vital Bab al-Mandeb Strait in two, giving Tehran de facto control over another key shipping route in addition to the Strait of Hormuz.

Earlier this week, a source told CNN that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had spoken twice with US President Donald Trump to urge him to strike the Houthis as the militia advances across Yemen toward the Red Sea, but that Trump declined.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Yemen's National Resistance Factions, military groups aligned with the Yemeni government, said Sunday that more than 500 of its fighters have been killed in the three-week Houthi offensive on Yemen's western coast.

Saudi Arabia said Saturday it temporarily closed its East-West pipeline as a precaution after a drone attack. Both Baghdad and Riyadh said the attack originated in Iraq, where Iranian-backed militias operate.

When asked about Saudi concerns after the pipeline closure and about moving marine traffic through the strait, Trump said that everything will "work out fine."

CNN's Jennifer Hansler and Max Saltman contributed to this report.
